missing_spec_content.spec_text: An example of how the growth of tourism in an LIC or NEE helps to reduce the development gap.
missing_spec_content.why: The tourism example is Kenya, but the lesson never identifies Kenya as an LIC or an NEE. keyPoints[1].content calls it "lower-middle income" and keyPoints[4].content calls it "a poorer country that is growing fast". Kenya is not on the lesson's own NEE list ("China, India, Brazil and Nigeria"). A student cannot see that the example meets the specification's LIC/NEE requirement.

above_gcse.text: In between are middle income countries, split into upper-middle and lower-middle. Kenya is lower-middle income
above_gcse.why: The specification works with LIC/NEE categories, and the lesson also uses HIC. Adding the World Bank upper-middle and lower-middle bands, and placing the case-study country in one of them, could confuse the student about which category to use in the exam.

above_gcse.text: Extreme poverty means living on less than $3 a day (in 2021 prices).
above_gcse.why: Neither the poverty-line definition nor the idea of fixed-year prices is in the specification sections. "In 2021 prices" refers to a purchasing-power-parity adjustment that is not explained and could confuse a 15-year-old.

above_gcse.text: The United Nations has set Sustainable Development Goals. These are targets for every country to end poverty and hunger and improve health and schooling.
above_gcse.why: The Sustainable Development Goals are not required by 3.2.2.1 or 3.2.2.2. This content, and the whole key point "Is the development gap closing?", goes beyond the specification text supplied.

factual_errors.text: Raw materials sold before anything is made from them, such as crops, oil or metal ores. They earn far less than manufactured goods.
factual_errors.correction: As a blanket statement this is misleading, especially with oil as the example, because oil exports earn some countries very large sums. The accurate point is that primary products usually have low value added and unstable prices, so countries that rely on them tend to earn less and less reliably than countries exporting manufactured goods.

not_checked: Diagram "g5-brandt-line" (keyPoints[1].diagram and keyPoints[1].pictures) could not be seen. Its labels ("NORTH — richer", "SOUTH — poorer", "Japan", "Australia", "NZ") suggest the usual layout, but where the line is drawn could not be checked.

The 2025 GNI per head figures in keyPoints[0].content and keyPoints[1].content ("$88,810 in the USA, $54,550 in the UK, $1,360 in Nigeria and $750 in Niger", "$2,200 in 2025") are dated later than data available to me. They are plausible in scale but could not be verified.

The 2024 life expectancy and infant mortality figures ("about 84 years in Japan and 55 in Nigeria"; intro: "about 2 babies in every 1,000" in Japan, "about 70 in every 1,000" in Nigeria) are plausible but could not be checked against the cited 2024 data.
The extreme poverty figures in keyPoints[5].content ("from about 43% in 1990 to about 10% in 2024") depend on the World Bank's revised $3.00 line. They are plausible but not verified.

The HIPC statement in keyPoints[4].content ("most of the 39 poor countries that qualified have had much of their debt cancelled") is consistent with my knowledge, but the source note's count of 36 could not be checked. My own knowledge suggests 37 had reached completion point after Somalia in 2023.

The Grameen Bank and Kenya tourism figures in keyPoints[4].content ("about 1.2 million ... in 2015 and about 2 million in 2019", "$1.76 billion, about 15%") are plausible but were not verified against the cited sources.
